--- title: "Application exercise 2: Training error will lie to you" subtitle: "STA 363 | Meeting 2 | August 28" toc-depth: 2 execute: echo: true editor: source jupyter: python3 --- ## Setup ::: {#983dc903 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error DATA = "https://lucymcgowan.github.io/sta-363-f26/data/" Auto = pd.read_csv(DATA + "Auto.csv") Auto.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: We will predict `mpg` from `horsepower`. ::: {#e8ecdcf4 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} X = Auto[["horsepower"]] y = Auto["mpg"] ``` ::: ## Part 1: Look before you model ::: {#3516ffac .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5)) ax.scatter(X["horsepower"], y, s=12, alpha=0.6, color="#d5008f") ax.set_xlabel("horsepower") ax.set_ylabel("mpg") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](02-ex_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ::: {.question} Would a straight line be a good description of this relationship? Sketch, in words, the shape you see. ::: ::: {.answer-space} ::: ## Part 2: Split Fill in the blank so that 30% of the observations are held out. ::: {#8f14d3cc .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split( X, y, test_size=____, random_state=363 ) ``` ::: ::: {.question} Why does `random_state` matter? What would change if you left it out? ::: ::: {.answer-space} ::: ## Part 3: Training MSE versus test MSE ::: {#d6cd626b .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} degrees = range(1, 11) train_mse, test_mse = [], [] for d in degrees: model = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(d), LinearRegression()) model.fit(X_train, y_train) train_mse.append(mean_squared_error(y_train, model.predict(X_train))) test_mse.append(mean_squared_error(y_test, model.predict(X_test))) ``` ::: ::: {#6d60f2d6 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} pd.DataFrame({"degree": degrees, "train": train_mse, "test": test_mse}).round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: {.question} 1. Which degree minimizes **training** MSE? Is that surprising? 2. Which degree minimizes **test** MSE? 3. At which degree do the two columns start to disagree about the direction of improvement? What is happening there? ::: ::: {.answer-space} ::: ## Part 4: Plot it ::: {#72078373 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5)) ax.plot(degrees, train_mse, "-o", color="#595959", label="Training MSE") ax.plot(degrees, test_mse, "-o", color="#d5008f", label="Test MSE") ax.set_xlabel("Polynomial degree") ax.set_ylabel("MSE") ax.legend() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](02-ex_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ::: {.question} Compare this to Figure 2.9 in the textbook. Which of the three panels (Figures 2.9, 2.10, 2.11) does the `Auto` data most resemble? What does that tell you about the true $f$? ::: ::: {.answer-space} ::: ## Part 5: The uncomfortable part Re-run everything above with `random_state=1`, then `random_state=2`, then `random_state=3`. Record the best degree each time. ::: {.question} | `random_state` | best degree | test MSE at that degree | |---|---|---| | 363 | | | | 1 | | | | 2 | | | | 3 | | | ::: ::: {.question} How much did your answer move? If a colleague reported "the best model is degree 7" based on one split, how much would you trust them? ::: ::: {.answer-space} ::: ::: {.takeaway} Hold on to this. It is the reason cross-validation exists, and we will build it in two weeks. ::: *Data from James, G., Witten, D., Hastie, T., Tibshirani, R., and Taylor, J. (2023).
